docs.abstract: President Dilma Rousseff on Friday vetoed portions of Brazil’s new Forest Code, a bill drafted to open big areas of protected forests to large-scale agriculture.
docs.snippet: President Dilma Rousseff on Friday vetoed portions of Brazil’s new Forest Code, a bill drafted to open big areas of protected forests to large-scale agriculture.
docs.lead_paragraph: President Dilma Rousseff on Friday vetoed portions of Brazil’s new Forest Code, a bill drafted to open big areas of protected forests to large-scale agriculture. The decision by Ms. Rousseff, which removes 12 articles from the bill, alters legislation sought by powerful agricultural groups. The bill had provoked outrage among environmentalists, some business leaders and cultural icons, especially over a provision that effectively granted amnesty to landowners who illegally deforested some areas. Responding to these concerns, Environment Minister Izabella Teixeira said the president’s line-item vetoes ruled out amnesty. Still, Ms. Rousseff’s action fell short of the expectations of environmental groups, which had wanted her to veto the entire bill. Details about the changes to the bill were sparse on Friday, with Brazil’s powerful Agriculture and Livestock Confederation withholding comment. The official text of Ms. Rousseff’s alterations, which include dozens of suggested changes to the bill in addition to the vetoed portions, is expected to be published on Monday.

headline.main: Brazil: President Vetoes Major Parts of Bill to Open Up Forests

docs.lead_paragraph: Gran Eléctrica, in Brooklyn’s Dumbo neighborhood, is a brick-walled, votive-lighted, tin-ceilinged amalgam of the sustainably local and the whimsically loco. The mescal beverage options promise to knock your Birkenstocks off, as does the back garden, where the Brooklyn Bridge curves overhead like a distant awning. Set in a landmarked 1835 brick building that began as a purveyor of fire insurance to the shipping trade, the restaurant, at 5 Front Street, is owned by the group that brought Colonie to Brooklyn Heights last year. The chef, Sam Richman, honed his haute French technique at Jean Georges and Per Se but spent a month in Mexico on a culinary cram course before taking over the kitchen. Pacifico Clara beer ($6) makes its New York City debut on tap. About those skulls and skeletons on the walls: the Día de los Muertos motif of the Mexican artist José Guadalupe Posada has been customized in Dumbo-centric wallpaper. It works its intended macabre magic.

docs.lead_paragraph: C. B. Bucknor, 50, was a physical therapist at what was then New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center when, on a whim, he used vacation time to attend umpire school in 1990. A career change ensued. Now, most of his Sundays involve ballgames and airline travel; he umpires 135 Major League games a season, not counting spring training and the playoffs. (He has worked the playoffs three times, but never a World Series, and his calls have sometimes been controversial.) In the off-season he spends time in his hometown, Savanna-la-Mar, Jamaica, where he helps run an annual “Treat 54” party (named for his uniform number) for local children. docs.lead_paragraph: Jurors in the corruption trial of John Edwards ended their sixth day of deliberations without reaching a verdict and will not come back to court until Tuesday because of the holiday weekend. Before dismissing the jury, Judge Catherine C. Eagles briefly cleared the courtroom of spectators to discuss a “juror issue” with the prosecution and defense lawyers. Once she reopened court, she warned the jurors to discuss the case only when the full complement of 12 was present. “You shouldn’t talk about the case in small groups,” she said. She also planned to resume court at 9 a.m. in case the jury issue needed more attention. Jury behavior has drawn attention in recent days. On Thursday, the four alternate jurors came to court in yellow shirts. On Friday, they wore red. Two of the women alternates also giggled and glanced at Mr. Edwards, prompting speculation by courtroom observers that at least one of them was flirting.

docs.lead_paragraph: When 3,000 reserved-seat tickets to the Belmont Stakes were made available online Monday after I’ll Have Another won the Preakness to keep his Triple Crown bid alive, they were snatched up in about three minutes. docs.lead_paragraph: The back story to my Sunday column is that I’ve always been interested in Memuna, because she’s a wonderful example of how an individual story and photos can galvanize the political will to end atrocities. (I’ve tried to use a similar approach to call attention and galvanize opposition to atrocities in other parts of the world, with mixed success.) That visit by Madeleine Albright, and the photos of her holding Memuna — as well as photos of other amputees — helped build the international resolve to defeat the rebellion and eventually prosecute Charles Taylor for crimes against humanity.

headline.main: Reader Comments on the Girl Who Symbolizes…Resilience!

Liukin, the reigning Olympic champion in the all-around, gracefully flipped, twisted and split-jumped above the four-inch beam, receiving a score of 14.9, good enough to tie for third with Sarah Finnegan. docs.lead_paragraph: The face never comes into view in my dreams, but I know it’s him. The twisted mouth is agape, molded in an eternal gasp of shock. The lower half of his body is gone, and there’s a black hole where his guts should have been. When Chevy was blown from the Stryker hatch, he took flight for an incalculable measure of time before landing on the slat armor of his vehicle. His uniform was blown off, which never happens in the movies. But he was whole, as complete and pure as the day he was born, I’m told. docs.abstract: The conflict is not one between motherhood and feminism, but within feminism itself.
docs.snippet: The conflict is not one between motherhood and feminism, but within feminism itself.
docs.lead_paragraph: The “mommy wars” have flared up once again, sparked most recently by the publication of the English translation of Elisabeth Badinter’s book, “The Conflict:  How Modern Motherhood Undermines the Status of Women.” In it, Badinter argues that a certain contemporary style of mothering — a style that requires total devotion of mother to child, starting with natural childbirth and extending through exclusive and on-demand breastfeeding, baby-wearing and co-sleeping — undermines women’s equality.  Badinter claims that it does this in several ways:  by squeezing fathers out of any meaningful role in parenting; by placing such high demands on mothers that it becomes nearly impossible to balance paid work with motherhood (especially once fathers have been sidelined); and by sending the message that day care, bottle feeding, sleep training and the other things that allow women to combine motherhood with paid work are harmful to children, and that the women who use them are selfish.

headline.main: ‘Mommy Wars’ Redux:  A False Conflict

One, they — that is, the people of “60 Minutes” — must have come up with this ultra positive story on the city that Lonely Planet ranks “the third hottest” in the world to compensate for the negative and very controversial story on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian Christians they broadcast in April. docs.snippet: Malt & Mold on the Lower East Side may be out of the way, but it is the only local retailer for knishes from Knishery NYC, salami by Charlito’s Cocina and ice cream from the Bent Spoon.
docs.lead_paragraph: Suppose you are deep downtown, where Canal Street and the Lower East Side disappear into blocks of apartments past Seward Park, and you crave a beer. No, not just a Corona, but maybe something artisanal, like Ithaca Beer, from upstate. Kevin M. Heald’s smartly tailored little shop, Malt & Mold, is there to help. With his beard and hat, Mr. Heald (shown), 43, looks every bit the monger of cheese and beer he calls himself. He has assembled about 50 craft beers, mostly domestic, and a well-curated assortment of cheeses, also artisanal and American, along with some imports like taleggio. Pickles and chocolates from Brooklyn, yogurts, vinegars, crackers and cured meats line the shelves and display cases. For now, the beers are in bottles and cans; eight tap lines, and growlers in various sizes, await a state permit. The shop may be out of the way, but it is the only local retailer for the excellent sweet and savory knishes from Knishery NYC, a new company; for salami by Charlito’s Cocina, of Long Island City, Queens; and for ice cream from the Bent Spoon, of Princeton, N.J., which shares the freezer with Blue Marble, Adirondack and Van Leeuwen.

headline.main: Brews and Bites Off the Usual Track

docs.lead_paragraph: So, the De Beers Talisman Crown is way out of your price range. There’s another decadent (and delicious) way to partake in Queen Elizabeth II’s Diamond Jubilee this weekend — with a box of special-edition truffles from the queen’s official chocolatier, Prestat. Awarded the royal warrant by Her Majesty in 1975, Prestat was first established in 1902 and has accompanied the British monarch on everything from business trips to family holidays aboard the Royal Yacht Britannia. The Jubilee box, designed by the royal florist Kitty Arden, features a cheery illustration that incorporates the Union Jack, a gold coronation state carriage, a unicorn and the queen’s favorite corgis. (She’s owned more than 30 since being given her first, named Susan, on her 18th birthday.) Flavors include 1895 Gianduja, Marc de Champagne and Earl Grey. Sweet!

headline.main: The Get | Prestat’s Diamond Jubilee Truffles

docs.lead_paragraph: It would be an overstatement to say that the whole wide world was watching when Bob Dylan’s ship came in, but surely his fans pinched themselves and squealed and knew that it was for real when he was awarded a Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Dylan, 71, whose career of more than 50 years stretches from early folk songs like “The Times They Are A-Changin'” and “When the Ship Comes In” to the recondite rock of recent albums like “Modern Times” and “Together Through Life,” was presented with the medal at a ceremony in the White House, where President Obama said of him, “There is not a bigger giant in the history of American music.” Mr. Obama also praised Mr. Dylan’s voice for its “weight” and “unique gravelly power” that redefined “not just what music sounded like but the message it carried and how it made people feel.”

headline.main: Bob Dylan Among Recipients of Presidential Medal of Freedom

docs.abstract: The blazing Texas sun is at the heart of the artist Jason Glasser’s new show in Williamsburg.
docs.snippet: The blazing Texas sun is at the heart of the artist Jason Glasser’s new show in Williamsburg.
docs.lead_paragraph: The blazing sun is at the heart of the artist Jason Glasser‘s mesmerizing new show, “Lone Star,” which is on view through June 10 at Parker’s Box in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. Born in Connecticut, Glasser lives in Paris with his wife, who’s French. But his latest work sprouted out of the year they just spent in Texas — a “self-imposed exile,” Glasser called it, intended to help his young children learn English. That sojourn produced a trippy silent film, streaming above, which was made around Barton Springs, a popular place to swim in Austin. In the exhibition, this film is projected onto a concave piece of glass that was once a television screen. “My tourist-grade camera does some interesting things when the sun reflects off the water so intensely,” Glasser said. “The images in this film have not been manipulated other than what I got just using my camera.”

headline.main: Now Showing | ‘Lone Star’

docs.lead_paragraph: You don’t have to be Stephen King to find small-town amusement parks inherently terrifying, but that author sees enough suspense in the environs of a 1970s-era carnival – and all the rusty arcade attractions and rickety roller coasters that suggests – to set a new novel there. On Wednesday the Hard Case Crime imprint of Titan Books plans to announce that it will publish “Joyland,” a new work of fiction by Mr. King, whose protagonist is a college student working at a North Carolina theme park in the summer of 1973. While employed there the character “confronts the legacy of a vicious murder, the fate of a dying child, and the ways both will change his life forever,” the publisher said in a news release. Charles Ardai, the Hard Case Crime editor, said in a statement that “Joyland” is “a whodunit, it’s a carny novel, it’s a story about growing up and growing old, and about those who don’t get to do either because death comes for them before their time.”

headline.main: New Stephen King Thriller Coming Next June

docs.lead_paragraph: A parcel containing a severed human foot was delivered to the headquarters of the governing Conservative Party of Canada on Tuesday. Fred DeLorey, a spokesman for the party, said that “a suspicious package was sent to our office” but referred all other questions to the police. Meola was a transitional figure in soccer in the United States, bridging the gap between an era when few followed the national team to one it which it drew 100,000 people to the Rose Bowl for a World Cup match. docs.abstract: A launch pad for downtown artists gets a retail space.
docs.snippet: A launch pad for downtown artists gets a retail space.
docs.lead_paragraph: Back in 1999, before retail moved in and skinny jeans became the neighborhood’s de facto uniform, the hippest place on the Lower East Side was Alife, a sneaker shop-cum-gallery on Orchard Street that served as both clubhouse and launch pad for a generation of downtown artists, including Steve Powers, a k a ESPO; Ryan McGinley; and Dash Snow. Two of Alife’s founders, Rob Cristofaro and Arnaud Delecolle, have since gone on to found a design agency called New York Art Department, under the guise of which they’ve taken on a new retail project: the Hole Shop at the Hole Gallery. “The idea is to bring some of what we were doing at Alife, before the scene was appropriated and commercialized, and apply it to what’s going on today,” Delecolle explains. The merchandise includes books, T-shirts, Polaroid cameras from the Impossible Project, Krink markers and sustainable furniture made by the Brooklyn design firm Uhuru. Since taking over the Bowery space a couple of months ago, NYAD has also hosted book-release parties — the French graffiti artist FAFI dropped by last week to sign copies of her first comic book — as well as film screenings and a 24-hour-a-day curated video screen that’s currently under the auspices of Luck You, a collective of teenage artists who work out of a loft in Chinatown. Continuing Delecolle and Cristofaro’s tradition of introducing new artists to wider audiences, on June 1 they’re curating their first show at the Hole Gallery. It will feature the work of a graffiti artist known only as Jim Joe, whose combination of anonymity, ubiquity (Jim Joe’s cryptic tags are all over the East Village and the Lower East Side) and epigrammatic use of social media has spurred a cult following. “Jim Joe is one of those artists who have one foot in the graffiti world and one foot in something weirder and more conceptual,” says Kathy Grayson, the Hole’s founder. “I’m really excited to see what he comes up with for his first gallery exhibition. I’m sure that it will capture the odd humor and serendipitous, random mischievousness of what he does in public places, and I get the sense that he is sophisticated enough to make it work in a new way in a gallery space. I would definitely say that this is a very hotly anticipated show as no one knows who he is and everyone wants to see what he does next.”

headline.main: New Digs | The Hole Shop at the Hole Gallery

docs.lead_paragraph: As part of its 2012 report on rent affordability, the National Low Income Housing Coalition released a chart that’s been floating around the Internet. It shows that there isn’t a single state in the country where it’s possible to work 40 hours per week at minimum wage and afford a two-bedroom apartment at Fair Market Rent. In West Virginia and Arkansas, you’d need to work at least a 63-hour week, and that’s as good as it gets. In California, Maryland, D.C., New Jersey and New York you’d need to work 130 hours or more. Hawaii comes in last place: 175 hours.

docs.abstract: From garden to table, in minutes: Carlos Suarez teams up with Wade Moises, formerly of Eataly, to create Italian food with ingredients grown from the restaurant’s organic rooftop garden.
docs.snippet: From garden to table, in minutes: Carlos Suarez teams up with Wade Moises, formerly of Eataly, to create Italian food with ingredients grown from the restaurant’s organic rooftop garden.
docs.lead_paragraph: When the restaurateur Carlos Suarez (owner of Bobo) was away at English boarding school, he missed the rustic meals cooked by his mother, Rosemary. “My father had his own business, so he worked a lot,” Suarez said. “Family dinner was our opportunity to sit together and enjoy her cooking: salads with tomatoes or avocados from the garden, shepherd’s pie and schnitzel (she’s English with an Austrian background).” Now living in a house with an olive grove in Lucca, Italy, Rosemary’s specialties have since changed, and it comes as no surprise that her son has named his new Italian restaurant in her honor. In the space that once housed Cushman’s, then Sutter’s Bakery, Suarez has Wade Moises, former chef de cuisine of Eataly, overseeing a kitchen that makes fresh pasta and focacce, as well as seasonal dishes prepared with ingredients grown on the restaurant’s organic rooftop garden. (The day’s harvest gets dropped down to the dining room in a basket on a block and tackle.) “It’s an opportunity to bring the source of the food literally a flight of stairs away from your dining table,” said Suarez, who plans to give students from the local Public School 41 tours and lessons on “how to turn those vegetables into lunch. We’re hoping to offer generosity, camaraderie and engagement — a sense of community,” he said. There’s another unusual aspect to the joint. Beyond the reclaimed wooden table tops, Suarez has gone green with a Dekar Design interior: “Instead of filling space with taxidermy and black and white photos, we used nature as our décor.” Inside are towers of artichokes and lemons, even “little Dr. Seuss” blueberry trees. Outside, the roof will also soon feature a beehive and chicken coop.

headline.main: Table Talk | Rosemary’s in Manhattan

docs.lead_paragraph: Founded by Julia Leach, a former executive vice president and creative director for Kate Spade, Chance is a T-shirt company turned total-lifestyle brand. Take Leach’s latest “California” collection (her second), for example. It includes not only a group of simple and thoughtfully designed striped tees in fresh West Coast colors, but also all of the things that support a summer well spent wearing them: sheared cotton towels that read “Seashore” and “Poolside,” espadrilles, Turkish “foutas” (multi-use textiles) and straw fedoras, to start. This month the designer adds yet another must-have to the mix — a limited edition long-sleeve style featuring a wiggly stripe hand-drawn by the artist Elliott Puckette, a friend of Leach’s. “I wanted the shirt to appear to be a canvas,” Leach says. “I didn’t want trims or excessive stitching to interfere with the grace of the lines.” Available in four colors — soft black, pink, sky blue and pool blue — the Pima cotton tees echo Puckette’s preferred palette. For her, the design process began as ink on paper. “Ordinarily I etch the lines in my paintings, which is fairly laborious and slow,” she says. “I found the process of drawing these lines instead very meditative and fluid.” Here, the artist Leanne Shapton surrounds herself with all four. Wouldn’t you?

headline.main: The Get | Chance’s Elliott Stripe Tees

docs.abstract: The practice of Forest Service officers’ requesting language interpretation and security backup from Border Patrol agents during stops of Spanish-speaking people is discriminatory, according to a ruling made public this week.

docs.lead_paragraph: The practice of Forest Service officers’ requesting language interpretation and security backup from Border Patrol agents during stops of Spanish-speaking people is discriminatory, according to a federal administrative ruling made public this week. The ruling, by Joe Leonard Jr., the assistant secretary for civil rights of the Department of Agriculture, said requesting interpretation assistance was “merely an excuse to target Latino individuals for immigration enforcement.” The ruling came in response to a claim by the companion of a Mexican man who drowned in a river on the Olympic Peninsula of Washington last year after a Border Patrol officer, summoned by a Forest Service officer, chased the man into the woods. The couple had been stopped on national forestland while picking salal, an evergreen shrub used in floral arrangements. The ruling included disciplinary actions against some employees, and it ordered the Forest Service to create new guidelines for dealing with people who speak limited English.

headline.main: Washington: Ruling Against Border Patrol Backup

docs.lead_paragraph: In this essay, adapted from his book “America the Philosophical,” Carlin Romano rebuts the common charge — shared by Tocqueville — that American culture is essentially anti-philosophical. That’s only true, he says, if we think of philosophical engagement as the academy would have us, namely, as tantamount to knowledge of the Western philosophical canon. While it’s true that Americans are less familiar with that canon than some of their European counterparts, it needn’t be true that they are philosophically averse, so long as we take philosophy not to inhere in any body of knowledge, or in the application of any particular method — conceptual analysis, phenomenology and so forth — but rather in an imaginatively critical cast of mind. Taken this way, America turns out to be the most philosophical culture on the planet.

headline.main: Stone Links: Philosophy, American Style

Almost on cue, two groundskeepers roll silently by in a modified golf cart picking up small twigs and limbs. They give a jaunty wave and move on. docs.abstract: In this town, it starts with learning. Centuries of it. But if that’s too tweedy for you, don’t worry. You can also find Harry Potter, Michelin-starred dining, live music and more.
docs.snippet: In this town, it starts with learning. Centuries of it. But if that’s too tweedy for you, don’t worry. You can also find Harry Potter, Michelin-starred dining, live music and more.
docs.lead_paragraph: OXFORD is not a college town — it is the college town. Its namesake university’s 38 colleges are so steeped in scholarly history they make Harvard and Yale seem like baby-faced freshmen. To wit: Oxford’s New College was last considered “new” in the 14th century. (Even the obsolete term “New World” is newer.) Students here get into the act, many dressing in tweed coats, sometimes even with elbow patches, and ordering pints of cask ale at pubs that have been in business for nearly four-fifths of a millennium. But Oxford has a modern side, too: night spots blare house and electronic music; restaurants serve modern takes on local food and exotic ethnic cuisine; and comfortable boutique hotels and bed-and- breakfasts beat medieval lodging houses for comfort any day. (Just don’t ask for a place to hitch your horse.)

headline.main: 36 Hours in Oxford, England

docs.lead_paragraph: I’m not sure this counts as a spoiler of anything other than Universal’s sleek and seductive marketing campaign — which has properly emphasized crows, swords and Charlize Theron’s hair — but there are actually some dwarfs in the new movie “Snow White and the Huntsman.” The small fellows who befriend the exiled princess here are nothing like the grumpy, sneezy, dopey guys you remember from the Disney version. The actors who play them (including Ian McShane, Eddie Marsan, Ray Winstone and the great Bob Hoskins, all digitally shrunken) might otherwise have been assembled for a nasty little Cockney gangster film. These dwarfs are industrious, but they don’t whistle while they work. Their most memorable song is a haunting dirge performed at the funeral pyre of a fallen comrade. So take note: There is nothing cute about this movie.

docs.snippet: Who is the greatest racehorse of all time? If superiority over contemporaries, enduring fame and influence on the breed are measures, no horse has surpassed Eclipse.
docs.lead_paragraph: Who is the greatest racehorse of all time? It is a fruitless but enjoyable debate. In America, you might argue for the pre-eminence of Lexington in the 19th century, and Secretariat in the 20th. Many of us in Europe would nominate St Simon (1881-1908) and Sea Bird II (1962-1973) from those centuries; we might also suggest that our current champion, Frankel, has the potential to join these ranks. But if superiority over contemporaries, enduring fame and influence on the breed are measures, no horse has surpassed Eclipse (1764-1789).

headline.main: On Cusp of History, Remembering One of the Greats

docs.snippet: “Antico: The Golden Age of Renaissance Bronzes,” at the Frick Collection, reveals a neo-Classical artist whose innovations were obscured by similar work from years later.
docs.lead_paragraph: Pier Jacopo Alari Bonacolsi (about 1455-1528) — or, as he was known, Antico, “the antique one” — was one of the most skilled and innovative sculptors of the early Italian Renaissance, celebrated during his lifetime for impeccably neo-Classical bronze statuettes of pagan heroes and gods. But his achievements were swamped and obscured by wave upon wave of generic desktop-size bronzes in the ensuing centuries, and his name was forgotten until early-20th-century art historians rediscovered him.

headline.main: Classics in the Palms of His Hands

docs.lead_paragraph: There is an unfortunate logic to bank runs.
